It is going to unfold over several months, more than a year, and the effects are different across different regions in different locations. So it's really important that national authorities work alongside the national met agencies, the regional centers, and of course at the global level with WMO to keep an eye on what is unfolding. Of course, we can anticipate many of the impacts based on analogous El Nino events in the past. But no two El Ninos are alike, so it is really important that our method of anticipating what will happen and how we will respond to what will happen is something which is very dynamic. It requires a coordination mechanism which is running for the next 12 to 18 months. The second message is that a lot of the times the focus is on one or two sectors very narrowly. And the most obvious one is agriculture. Of course, agriculture is affected very badly in many parts of the world. But the effects are actually really multi-sectorial. It is on availability of water. water, including drinking water. There are implications for energy production where reservoirs are running low and the hydropower electricity generation capacity may be compromised. It is for other infrastructure systems. For example, Panama Canal, you know, it is serviced by two reservoirs. If the water level is down there, it affects the traffic. But all of it is something that we can anticipate and we can prepare. So my second message is that it is really important that countries take a multi-sectorial approach in addressing this and the United Nations system stands ready to support that effort. And the third point is that it's really important that we focus on local level and really identify communities and locations that are more vulnerable than the others. And we do not apply approach which is same for every place, for every community, because some of the impacts are really focused in some locations for some people. Uh, the impact could be much higher. Statelessness falls within UNHCR's mandate. We've been tasked by the General Assembly with a responsibility to identify and protect stateless people and also to help states to prevent and reduce statelessness. So there is clearly progress, and we know how that progress can be achieved. However, discrimination continues to be a major concern for statelessness. In 24 countries, women cannot confer nationality to their children on an equal basis with women. That needs to change. Some nationality laws still lack safeguards for children who would otherwise be stateless. Elsewhere, safeguards exist on paper, but they're not applied in practice. We also have cases of arbitrary deprivation of nationality, which is also a serious concern. So today, UNHCR is asking for four concrete things. that states should protect stateless persons that are on their territory and establish clear pathways through which they can acquire a nationality. Secondly, we would like to see those discriminatory nationality laws reformed so that every child can acquire a nationality. Thirdly, those legal frameworks, those two conventions, We would like all states to accede to those conventions to protect stateless persons on their territory, but also to find solutions for them. And then fourthly, there is a global alliance which is made-up of member states and civil society groups, UN agencies, which is working on practical solutions to support stateless persons, but also to help stateless persons acquire or reaffirm their nationality.
